clue.text: One involved in sad, mad, misguided avant-garde movement

indicators.note: something involved in a group is caught up inside it, so one piece sits within the others
misguided means led astray, so the letters wander out of their order and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is caught up in a gloomy, crazy and ill-judged arty movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman I goes among the letters of sad and mad, and the seven letters are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Dada was an early twentieth-century anti-art movement, and its ideas and practice are called Dadaism.

clue.text: A lot of people went by car

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a crowd or large moving mass
second meaning: past tense of a verb for driving a vehicle

explanation.surface: A crowd of folk made their journey by motor.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a herd or great crowd moving together, while the verb is the past tense of operating a motor vehicle.

clue.text: This old model is pretty stupid

indicators.note: to model is to shape or mould, so the preceding letters are reshaped into a new form

explanation.surface: An ageing fashion model is said to be rather dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' reads as a noun describing someone old; it is a verb telling you to remould THIS OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: A dolt is a dim, slow-witted person, so behaving like one is to be quite unintelligent.

clue.text: I controlled the country

parts.note: to run a business is to control it

explanation.surface: A dictator boasts of having governed the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Iran is a nation of the Middle East, formerly known as Persia, so it is one example of a country.

clue.text: Doctor Parson's medicine for mental illness?

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the following letters are altered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A physician called Parson prescribes a remedy for a psychiatric disorder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a title for Parson, but it is a verb telling you to rearrange all fifteen letters of the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic depression is the older name for bipolar disorder, a psychiatric condition of alternating high and low moods.

clue.text: German deviously tapes first of our secret policemen

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for German

indicators.note: acting deviously means taking a crooked route, so these letters are twisted out of order
the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

explanation.surface: A sly German records our spies and secret agents on tape.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gestapo was the secret state police of Nazi Germany, a force of undercover officers.

clue.text: A former French President cast Deng as rigid revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters before it are overturned into a new order

explanation.surface: A one-time French leader portrayed the Chinese leader Deng as an inflexible revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' reads as a verb of the President's, but it is part of the fodder, along with Deng Xiaoping's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing was head of state of France from 1974 to 1981.

clue.text: Drunken Denis surrounded by terrible dross and squalor

indicators.note: one thing surrounded by another sits inside it, so one group goes within the other
a drunken person staggers about, so the letters of the name lurch into a new order
something terrible is in a dreadful state, so the following word is mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A drunk called Denis lies amid awful rubbish in filthy surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two anagram signals, one per name: each word is rearranged on its own before one is set inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a filthy, wretched condition; squalor and sordidness are near synonyms for dirty degradation.

clue.text: Go on, propose!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: move forward or progress
second meaning: put forward an idea or suggestion

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like someone urging a suitor to pop the question; the two phrases are separate meanings of one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to move forward or proceed and to put forward a theory or suggestion for consideration.

clue.text: Take bird from Bangor to Lancaster

indicators.note: taking something from a phrase lifts it out of the words that follow, which contain it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first place name, the little word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Instructions to carry a bird on a journey between two British towns.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a route from Bangor in Wales to Lancaster in England; the bird sits inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: The ortolan is a small European bunting, famously eaten as a delicacy in France.

clue.text: Clumsily, Iona spilt the artist's materials

indicators.note: doing something clumsily makes a mess of it, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A clumsy girl named Iona knocked over a painter's supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil paints are pigments bound in linseed oil, a standard medium used by painters on canvas.

clue.text: Contrive to find part of pin

indicators.note: only a part of the preceding words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: a run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone tries to locate a section of a pin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' seems to point at the pin, but it points back at the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A rivet is a metal bolt or fastening hammered through holes to join plates, a kind of short metal peg.

clue.text: Throw out broken item

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, which can be put back in another order

explanation.surface: Someone discards a damaged object.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to send out or discharge, as a chimney gives off smoke, matching the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Cause Arsenal to lose heart? That's rare!

parts.note: to occasion something is to cause it

indicators.note: losing its heart strips a word of its interior, so only its outside letters stay

parts.note: just the outside letters of the football club's name

explanation.surface: Making a football team become dispirited is something that seldom happens.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal is a London football club. Here the whole interior, not just one central letter, is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something occasional happens only now and then, so it is infrequent, which is one sense of the adjective given.

clue.text: Unable to speak the language, couple died

parts.note: a tongue is a language, as in mother tongue
to couple is to join or tie together
d is the abbreviation for died, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A pair who could not communicate in the local language passed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The language' ends the definition in the surface, but the definition stops at 'speak'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tongue-tied means being lost for words through shyness or nervousness, so silent and inarticulate.

clue.text: Select sweets, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the wanted word only needs to be pronounced like the clue word

explanation.surface: An instruction to pick out some confectionery.
explanation.walkthrough: Chews are soft, chewy sweets, sold in Britain as small wrapped candies.
explanation.definitionFit: To choose is to pick one option from several, an exact synonym of the verb meaning to pick out.

clue.text: Waste a lot of time in prison cell

parts.note: an eon is an immensely long age

explanation.surface: Someone fritters away years behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste a lot of time' reads as a verb phrase about idling, but waste is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is a dark underground jail chamber, typically beneath a castle, where captives were held.

clue.text: Small lumberjack is a hard worker

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a logger fells trees for timber

explanation.surface: A little tree-feller is a diligent grafter.
explanation.definitionFit: To slog is to labour persistently, so someone who keeps slogging away is a tireless toiler.

clue.text: The Church of England's supporting unpleasant causes

indicators.note: in a down entry, something supporting another piece sits below it, so it comes later

parts.note: CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England

explanation.surface: The established church is said to back nasty campaigns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Causes' sounds like campaigns the Church backs, but it is the noun for origins.
explanation.definitionFit: The sources of something are its origins or what brings it about, so the plural nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: I am taken aback by some original Japanese art

indicators.note: taken aback suggests stepping backwards, so the order of the two little words is turned round

parts.note: some of the word, its usual abbreviation
the two words read in the other order

explanation.surface: Someone is startled by a piece of authentic Japanese art.
explanation.walkthrough: Unusually, the reversal swaps whole words rather than letters, so reversing letter by letter leads nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the traditional craft from Japan of folding paper into decorative shapes such as cranes.

clue.text: Safeguard English nurse abroad

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: abroad can mean astray or all over the place, so these letters are scattered

explanation.surface: Protect a British nurse working overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensure is to make certain of something, securing it against failure, as a verb for protecting.

clue.text: Crash into piece of wall

parts.note: to ram is to drive into something forcefully
a part is a piece of a whole

explanation.surface: Someone smashes into a section of brickwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of wall' looks like one phrase; the definition is wall alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A rampart is a defensive embankment or fortification bank around a castle or town.

clue.text: Inuit's very out of place in Oxford, perhaps

indicators.note: letters out of place are not where they should be and must be moved into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: An Arctic visitor feels a stranger in an English city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Oxford' reads as the place; 'Oxford, perhaps' is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford is home to a famous ancient seat of learning, so it is one example of such an institution.

clue.text: Starts to approach maverick army doctor for bullets

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words
MO is a medical officer, the army's doctor

explanation.surface: A wounded soldier first goes to an unconventional medic for ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammo is the informal short form of ammunition, which includes rounds fired from guns.

clue.text: The Gallaghers' watering hole?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the rock band led by the brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher
second meaning: a fertile spot with water in a desert

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the brothers' local pub; the band name is also a desert spring.
explanation.definitionFit: The Britpop group fronted by the Gallagher brothers shares its name with a fertile desert spring where travellers drink.

clue.text: Giant spilt gore

indicators.note: something spilt is scattered about, so the letters land in a new order

explanation.surface: A huge monster sheds blood.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating monster of folklore, typically huge, so a fairy-tale colossus.

clue.text: It's like a raccoon skin, a bit itchy

parts.note: an animal's coat is its skin and fur

indicators.note: just a bit of the next word is used, here its first letter

explanation.surface: A raccoon-like pelt that feels slightly scratchy.
explanation.definitionFit: The coati is a long-snouted mammal of the Americas belonging to the same family as raccoons.

clue.text: Gelatin can be found in beaker

parts.note: something that can be found exists, or is
a beaker is a drinking glass

explanation.surface: A jelly-like substance turns up in a laboratory vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Isinglass is a pure gelatin obtained from fish bladders, used for clarifying beer and making jellies.

clue.text: Where last of trains get repaired down in Wiltshire

definitions.text: Where last of trains get repaired down in Wiltshire

indicators.note: something repaired is put back together, here in a fresh order
the last of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

explanation.surface: A Wiltshire town where old trains were mended in the railway workshops.
explanation.walkthrough: Swindon is a Wiltshire town that grew around the Great Western Railway's engineering works, so the whole clue also describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The town was home to the railway works where locomotives were built and overhauled for over a century.

clue.text: Get shot in a riot in poor neighbourhoods

indicators.note: a riot is wild disorder, so the letters are thrown into chaos and rearranged

explanation.surface: People are shot during unrest in deprived districts.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghettos are deprived, overcrowded urban districts, often occupied by one marginalised minority group.
